summary: A 1977 note on writing network addresses as a set of fields that can be extended by adding fields on the left or right, or by making fields bigger. It was motivated by a larger address space in the host and IMP interface.

plainLanguage.summary: Like a home address with street, city and country, this note says network addresses can grow by adding more parts.

questions: why do network addresses need fields
how can addresses grow over time
subtitle: Breaking network addresses into fields that can grow independently

tldr.problem: Network addressing grew rigid as networks expanded. The host-IMP interface changed from 2-bit host and 6-bit IMP fields to 8-bit and 16-bit, breaking applications that treated them as a single 8-bit number. Multi-network systems and multi-processor hosts needed more address hierarchy.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of treating network addresses as single numbers, represent them as named fields (Network/IMP/Host/Message-ID) separated by delimiters. Each field can grow independently, and new fields can be added on either end.
tldr.outcome: Applications can extend addressing for multinetwork interconnection (adding network fields on the left) and fine-grain host structure (adding fields on the right) without breaking existing assumptions.

today: RFC 730 is an early and largely theoretical note about addressing. The Internet Protocol (RFC 791 and later IPv6) eventually took a different approach: fixed hierarchical address spaces (IPv4 networks, CIDR, and IPv6 address architecture) rather than named fields. However, the principle of extensible address hierarchy remains central to Internet routing.

sections.title: The Addressing Problem
sections.content:
RFC 730 proposes breaking network addresses into named fields instead of treating them as single numbers. This solves three problems: host-IMP interface changes that grew individual fields, the need for wider addresses in multinetwork systems, and the desire to address subcomponents within a single host.

By using a field-based notation like NET:1/3/5/7 or HOST:6, applications become independent of how many bits each field consumes, leaving room for growth on either side of the hierarchy.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of calling a host by one number, give it an address with parts like a street address: you can add more parts or make parts bigger without confusing everyone.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content:
The ARPANET's original host-IMP interface used 2 bits for host and 6 bits for IMP. When this grew to 8 bits and 16 bits, old software that treated it as a single 8-bit number broke. Host 65 in the old scheme became 65537 in the new one, making it impossible for applications to read old configurations.

Interconnecting separate networks requires new address hierarchy at the top. Multiprocessor hosts need fine-grained addressing within a single network attachment point. Field-based addressing handles all three by letting fields grow, be added on the left for new scope, or be added on the right for fine structure.
sections.plainLanguage: When your city grows and you need a bigger postal code, a field-based address adapts. Without it, every application has to be rewritten.

sections.title: The Field-Based Scheme
sections.content:
Each address starts with a field name that indicates the scope: NET for network-scoped addresses, IMP for IMP-scoped, HOST for the local IMP, or MESSAGE-ID for message routing. Fields are decimal numbers separated by slashes.

The benefit is clear: NET:1/3/5/7 says "go to network 1, then IMP 3, then host 5, then message ID 7." An application can also say HOST:6 to mean "host 6 on my current IMP," letting the receiver fill in context without needing to parse a full path.
sections.plainLanguage: A field-based address starts by saying the most general thing (network or host), then adds more specific details separated by slashes, letting each part describe what level you're talking about.

sections.title: Where It Counts
sections.content:
The RFC notes that field notation will matter most where humans type addresses: TIP "open" commands, Telnet and FTP "connect" commands, the MAIL address field, and official host name lists. In most places where addressing is buried in protocol machinery, it will not surface.

The scheme does require a small shift in how software works: instead of assuming a fixed bit layout, it must parse named fields. This is tractable and makes the system resilient to future growth.
sections.plainLanguage: This matters mostly when a person types an address, like connecting to a remote computer. In the background, software can adapt to bigger address fields automatically.
